rules.text: A block's body (after if, for, def) must be indented 4 spaces. Python reads indentation as part of the code.
Numbers and text are different types. Turn a number into text with str() before joining with +.
Average = total divided by HOW MANY items, i.e. len(list), not a fixed number.
Watch the boundary: > means 'greater than', >= means 'greater than or equal to'.
Read the LAST line of an error first: the error type and explanation are there.
A test (assert) is a promise about how code behaves. Code is done when every test passes, edge cases included.
Change one thing, run the tests again. Guessing with many changes at once gets confusing.
APPROVE when the code is correct, readable, and its tests pass. Don't hold back good work.
REVISE when there is a bug, a missed edge case, or a risky habit. Point to the problem line.
Passwords and secret keys must never be written in code. Keep them in secret settings (environment variables).
ESCALATE to a senior developer when a change needs special permission or expertise (production servers, customer data).
Unsure what a variable holds? Print it with print() at a few points, then compare with what you expect.
range(n) stops at n-1. Many off-by-one bugs come from loop boundaries.
IndexError/KeyError means reading something that isn't there. Check the list length or dictionary key first.
Reproduce the bug with the smallest example you can before fixing it.
Every change is saved as a commit with a message explaining what changed and why.
New release causing errors in production? ROLL BACK to the last healthy version first, fix it afterwards.
Compare the numbers before and after a release. Don't roll back a healthy release: choose APPROVE to keep it running.
Big changes are released gradually and watched, not to every user at once.
Test the edge cases: empty lists, zero, negative numbers, capital letters, text with spaces.
A test that always passes (like assert True) tests nothing.
Every fixed bug gets a new test, so that bug never comes back.
New logic without tests = REVISE. Ask the author to add relevant tests.
Don't trust user input: check its type and range before using it.
Never print or store passwords and personal data in logs.
Code that sends data to an unknown address, or comes from an unknown account, must be ESCALATED to the SOC team.
Use libraries from the company's official sources, not random code copied from forums.
